item.title: Trump speaks highly of China visit, signaling continued positive momentum in ties: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 20:21:00
US President Donald Trump holds a news conference covering his recent trip to China, the Iran conflict and other issues in the White House briefing room on November 20, 2026. Photo: VCG US President Donald Trump reviewed the outcomes of his recent Asia-Pacific trip at a White House press conference on Friday local time, praising the warm reception he received in China during APEC and host city Shenzhen’s impressive development. Chinese observers said the positive signals from the US could help sustain the improving momentum in China-US relations and create more room for bilateral engagement. The two countries can achieve mutually beneficial cooperation, they said, provided they uphold the principles of equality, respect and mutual benefit, expand areas of cooperation, manage differences and keep bilateral ties on a steady and healthy track. Trump spoke favorably of Shenzhen's urban environment and infrastructure, describing the city as a striking example of rapid development. “It's immaculate. It's been built in a short period of time,” he said, adding that the city had been a fishing village about 40 years ago. Trump contrasted what he saw in Shenzhen with conditions in some US cities, criticizing their dirty roads, potholes, deteriorating infrastructure and crime. He said he had closely examined the roads and guardrails during his visit and expressed “great respect for the job they've done.” “Shenzhen's transformation from a small fishing village into a high-tech metropolis clearly made an impression on Trump, who may well have genuinely admired China's achievements in modernization,” said Zhang Tengjun, an associate research fellow at the Institute of American Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. On emerging technologies, Trump said the US and China could work together to establish safeguards for what he called “super intelligence,” while portraying the two countries as the only leading players in the field. He added that the US was leading and China was second, saying, “Whoever wins SI wins,” CBS News reported. At the same time, Trump stressed that the US would seek to keep data center investment and advanced technology within its borders. He said his administration would not allow American companies to build data centers overseas. Trump also signaled his administration would keep restrictions on advanced chip exports to China in place, while leaving open the possibility of selling only older-generation chips. Meanwhile, he acknowledged that if the US refuses to supply such chips, China will develop its own. Cui Fan, professor at the School of International Trade and Economics, University of International Business and Economics, analyzed that the US appears to be seeking a model in which the two countries jointly manage risks while Washington retains its technological advantage. On trade and counternarcotics, Trump repeatedly cited what he described as a 97 percent decline in fentanyl entering the US by sea, presenting it as a major outcome of cooperation with China. He also expressed hope for a comprehensive trade agreement with Beijing. Cui noted the fentanyl issue illustrates that pragmatic China-US cooperation can help tackle global public challenges and uphold shared public interests when common interests exist. However, the US administration’s transactional approach to trade means that negotiating leverage is likely to remain in service of his “America First” agenda, experts said. The China-Russia-US Heads of State Declaration Toward Peace, released on Thursday in Shenzhen, noted that the three leaders reaffirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” and agreed that the three countries would engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the Xinhua News Agency reported. Yet China's nuclear arsenal remains nowhere near the scale of those of the US and Russia, making trilateral negotiations at this stage neither fair nor realistic, Zheng said, adding that China has consistently advocated the complete prohibition and thorough destruction of nuclear weapons, with the ultimate goal of building a world free of nuclear weapons. This position was reiterated in China's national report on the implementation of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, released by the Foreign Ministry in April. The report states that China "has all along advocated the ultimate goal of the complete prohibition and thorough destruction of nuclear weapons," with the ultimate goal of realizing a world free of nuclear weapons.

item.title: EU reportedly nears new trade tool to restrict market access, but protectionism offers no guarantee of industrial strength: analysts
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 17:16:00
The European Union (EU) flags in front of EU headquarters in Brussels, Belgium. Photo: VCG The European Union is finalizing plans for a new trade tool that could allow it to swiftly retaliate against trade actions by other countries, potentially restricting access to its vast single market, Bloomberg reported on Friday, as Brussels steps up protectionist drive trying to shield European industries from foreign competition. Chinese analysts warned that the EU's growing reliance on trade barriers will backfire, imposing additional costs on European businesses while doing little to address the industrial weaknesses behind the bloc's declining competitiveness. The proposed tool, tentatively called "ReadyEU," would allow the bloc to block certain goods and services from entering its market of 450 million consumers. Although the proposals are not formally aimed at any particular country, Bloomberg linked them to Brussels' efforts to reduce its trade deficit with China. Beijing has repeatedly stressed that trade surpluses are a natural outcome of global industrial specialization and changing trade patterns, rather than something China deliberately pursues. The package, expected to be unveiled on December 9, also includes plans to make existing trade defense instruments more agile and diversify strategically important supplies through measures ranging from tariffs and quotas to investment in alternative supply chains, Bloomberg reported. The move comes amid mounting pressure within the EU to tighten trade restrictions on China. On Thursday, lawmakers from five political groups in the European Parliament urged the European Commission to move beyond its current sector-by-sector approach and adopt broader, more systematic trade defense measures against China, Euronews reported. The lawmakers called for "horizontal" tariffs and quotas to address what they described as Chinese “overcapacity”, along with strict local supply-chain content rules and harmonized customs controls. The developments point to a shift from case-by-case trade scrutiny toward broader, institutionalized defenses, driven by Europe's weakening industrial competitiveness and Brussels' efforts to strengthen economic integration, Li Guanjie, a research fellow at the Shanghai Academy of Global Governance and Area Studies, told the Global Times on Saturday. The measures are protectionist in nature, Li said, adding that Brussels is seeking to defend established industries while strengthening its bargaining power with China. However, differences in member states' economic interests could complicate implementation. The bloc’s policy push has accelerated in recent weeks. On November 17, Politico reported that Brussels was considering changes to its Enforcement Regulation to retaliate faster against China, as it develops a trade "kill switch." The discussions followed an October Franco-German proposal for a rapid-response tool to restrict access to the EU single market, according to Reuters. The push also extends to public procurement. The Financial Times reported that the European Commission was considering barring foreign companies found to have breached the Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR) in one public tender from bidding for contracts across the EU, preventing them from seeking tenders in other member states. The emerging EU policy framework suggests three mutually reinforcing approaches: faster retaliation, cross-sector trade restrictions and tighter public procurement scrutiny. Together, they could give Brussels greater control over market access, extending trade defenses beyond individual products and disputes, analysts said. Yet expanding trade defenses does not resolve the problems that have weakened Europe's industrial position. Li said the bloc's deeper challenge lies in upgrading its products and technologies, something trade barriers cannot accomplish by insulating existing industries from competition. Nor would tighter restrictions necessarily deliver the intended results. European consumers would face higher prices for imported products, while Chinese companies' growing local manufacturing presence could limit the effectiveness of conventional border measures, Li said. The risks extend to European manufacturers themselves. Restrictions affecting Chinese components, equipment and clean-energy products could increase production costs and complicate industrial upgrading, potentially undermining the industries Brussels seeks to protect, according to industry analysis. China's Ministry of Commerce said on October 29 that artificially restricting normal trade could violate WTO rules and would do nothing to improve the EU's industrial competitiveness. China firmly opposes the abuse of trade defense instruments and will take all necessary measures to safeguard its legitimate interests if the EU imposes discriminatory restrictions on Chinese products, the ministry said. The latest proposals come despite Beijing and Brussels seek to manage trade frictions through an established consultation mechanism. At their second round of China-EU Trade and Investment Consultations in October, both sides agreed to hold technical discussions on the Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR), address market access concerns and explore investment cooperation. A ministerial video conference is scheduled for January 2027, ahead of the next round of consultations in March. Europe's long-term industrial competitiveness hinges on technological upgrading, investment and productivity, rather than higher trade barriers. “China's manufacturing strengths and integrated supply chains can support Europe's industrial and green transitions, making cooperation with China, rather than protectionist confrontation, a more effective path to industrial renewal,” Li noted.

item.title: Those who bet against the Chinese economy will ultimately be proven wrong: People's Daily
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 15:34:00
Photo: VCG Those in the US and the West who publicly talk down China's economy - what are they really up to? Throughout this year, certain overseas media outlets and institutions have repeatedly taken aim at China's economy. At times, they play up a so-called "deflationary trap," asserting that China's economic growth is unsustainable; at other times, they hype a "China Shock 2.0," claiming that Chinese manufacturing poses a threat to global industries. While their specific narratives keep shifting, the pessimistic conclusion remains constant - as if it had been scripted all along. Behind these arguments lie their own calculations of self-interest and political gain: using the specter of a "China collapse" narrative to undermine confidence, and invoking a "China threat" narrative to justify imposing restrictions and containment. Yet, the reality is that the trajectory of China's economic development has never been, and will never be, determined by those who seek to talk it down. Pessimistic narratives - a rigged question with a predetermined answer Predicting the downfall of the Chinese economy is nothing new. Back in 2001, some figures in the West floated the "China collapse" theory, forecasting that factors such as China's accession to the World Trade Organization would lead to its "collapse" by 2011. As expected, the predicted collapse never materialized. In 2016, certain observers abroad claimed that a "hard landing" for the Chinese economy was "almost inevitable." In 2023, the Wall Street Journal declared that "China's 40-year boom is over." This year, a new parade of narratives has emerged, ranging from a "deflationary trap" and a "China shock 2.0" to the "spillover of a Chinese economic crisis." For decades, voices from abroad have predicted the downfall of the Chinese economy, only to be proved wrong time and again. The pessimistic narratives that have emerged this year generally fall into a few categories. One approach involves overgeneralization, extrapolating temporary difficulties into an overall crisis. In October, the Washington Post seized upon isolated indicators such as short-term fluctuations in real estate prices and soft consumer confidence to paint an unduly bleak picture of China's economic prospects. This argument ignores the inherent complexity of the economy as a whole, and its conclusions crumble under scrutiny. Another tactic involves shifting the terms of the debate, reframing competitive advantages in the marketplace as threats to the rest of the world. When Chinese new-energy vehicles gained global popularity, critics cried "overcapacity"; as the competitiveness of China's manufacturing sector grew, they invoked the specter of a "China Shock 2.0" Since technological progress and gains in efficiency are fundamental to market competition, why is it that when Chinese enterprises achieve them, they are suddenly recast as risks that must be guarded against? Others arrive at their conclusions before even looking at the facts; regardless of how China's economy develops, they keep singing the same tune of doom and gloom. If economic growth slows, they claim the growth model is unsustainable; if growth remains steady, they argue it is overly reliant on policy stimulus. When exports face pressure, they question the competitiveness of "Made in China"; when export performance is strong, they attribute it to overcapacity and weak domestic demand - no matter the scenario, they always manage to reach a negative conclusion. In this way, economic analysis becomes a rigged question with a predetermined answer, much like preparing a plate of dumplings solely for the sake of having an excuse to serve the vinegar, while the dumplings themselves remain completely hollow. Yet, this does not stop these critics from spouting nonsense and hurling baseless accusations. Making an issue of China's economy - a complex agenda Certain individuals in the US and the West frequently make an issue of China's economy, a subject that, upon closer inspection, reveals a more complex agenda. In March this year, the Office of the US Trade Representative initiated a "Section 301 investigation" into several economies, including China, citing so-called "structural excess capacity" in the manufacturing sector. The stated objective: to safeguard the US industrial base and encourage the "reshoring" of manufacturing. It is clear that this is an attempt to preserve an existing status quo that favors the US' own established interests. In the past, companies from certain developed nations held a dominant position in high-end manufacturing, while China occupied a place primarily in the mid-to-low end of the global industrial division of labor. Today, however, Chinese new-energy vehicles are reaching global markets, and the country is making continuous breakthroughs in machinery, equipment, and communications technology with an increasing number of Chinese enterprises emerging as prominent players on the international stage. The cake remains the same, but the people sharing it have changed, and those who previously enjoyed the largest portions are naturally feeling uneasy. Yet, does the competitiveness of Chinese enterprises automatically equate to "unfair competition"? Does the popularity of Chinese goods among consumers necessarily signify "overcapacity"? If, upon failing to compete, one simply accuses the other side of breaking the rules, doesn't that turn market competition into a game where only one party is permitted to win? Some politicians even exploit the "China issue" to serve their own domestic political agendas. By blaming the closure of domestic factories on a "China shock" and attributing a decline in their own competitiveness to a "China threat," they can deflect internal tensions while drumming up support for tariff barriers and trade restrictions. After all, it is far more convenient to shift the blame onto China than to explain one's own policy failures or the sluggish pace of industrial transformation to voters. Ultimately, some individuals harbor deep-seated prejudices against China. They refuse to acknowledge the achievements of China's development path, insisting instead on judging the country through their own narrow set of standards. They go to great lengths to talk China down, seeking to undermine confidence in its development and diminish its appeal, ending up trapped in a mindset where they reflexively view China with suspicion and disparagement. Given the interplay of these various factors, it is hardly surprising that such negative narratives have persisted for so long. Negative rhetoric cannot erase China's economic achievements The noise from those predicting a downturn cannot alter the solid achievements, genuine quality, and positive trajectory of China's high-quality economic development. In the first three quarters of this year, China's economy grew by 4.6 percent year-on-year, a performance that ranks among the best for major global economies. Over the first 10 months, the total value of imports and exports of goods rose by 20 percent year-on-year, with imports alone surging by 23.6 percent. The recently concluded 9th China International Import Expo attracted participants from 162 countries, regions, and international organizations, with 4,142 overseas enterprises taking part, setting a new record. On one hand, some claim that China's economy has lost its appeal; on the other, global businesses are "voting with their feet" by choosing to engage with China. It is self-evident which side carries more weight. Naturally, economic development is bound to encounter difficulties and challenges. The real estate market is still undergoing adjustment, consumer confidence requires a boost, and the industrial transformation and upgrading process involves complex, "hard-to-crack" issues. We have never shied away from these problems. To address the imbalance between strong supply and weak demand, we are implementing targeted initiatives to bolster consumption and expand domestic demand. To manage pressures in the real estate sector, we are adopting city-specific policies and accelerating the creation of a new development model for the industry. To navigate the transition between old and new growth drivers, we are fostering "new quality productive forces" tailored to local conditions, revitalizing traditional industries while nurturing emerging ones. Throughout our journey, it has been precisely this spirit - facing problems head-on, fearing no hardship, working diligently, and overcoming obstacles - that has carried us forward. Looking back, how many storms has the Chinese economy weathered over the years? From the impact of a once-in-a-century pandemic to external containment and suppression - it has navigated through countless challenges and forged ahead against the waves. The underlying strength of the Chinese economy stems, ultimately, from the composure and steadfastness of its leadership in the face of adversity, the hard work and dedication of its hundreds of millions of people, and a firm commitment to focusing on its own priorities. For an economy with an ultra-large market, a complete industrial system, and robust innovation capabilities, how much of a stir can a few voices of pessimism really create? The most powerful response to all the clamor lies precisely in this spirit of "seizing the day." Recently, the 2026 APEC meetings were successfully held in Shenzhen. While some abroad are busy building walls and barriers or hyping up "threats," China is working with others to lay the foundations and framework for an Asia-Pacific community. By promoting the alignment of regional economic and trade agreements and fostering an open, innovation-driven ecosystem, China has taken a series of pragmatic steps, rooted in the Asia-Pacific but with a global vision, that not only serve the long-term common development of the region but also pave a new path toward building a community with a shared future for humanity. "No matter how the international landscape may evolve, China will not waver in its pursuit of win-win cooperation with all other countries." The global economic pie can only grow larger through concerted cooperation. On one side lies the narrow-minded approach of zero-sum games and protectionism; on the other, a broad-minded commitment to openness, inclusiveness, and mutually beneficial cooperation. Who treats the global economy as an arena for a "win-lose" contest, and who is striving to broaden the path toward common development? When the two are contrasted, the truth becomes self-evident. Those who talk down the economy will ultimately be proven wrong, while those who engage in concrete action can look forward to a bright future.

item.title: Nvidia plunges 14% amid SEC probe; mounting US scrutiny could cast long shadow over chip giant: analysts
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 14:29:00
The Nvidia logo is displayed on a smartphone, with the company's former CEO Jensen Huang in the background. Photo: VCG Nvidia shares plunged again on Friday after reports of a US securities investigation into potential accounting issues rattled investors. Analysts warned that mounting regulatory pressure, driven partly by Washington's zero-sum mindset toward technology competition with China, could pose lasting risks to Nvidia's business and global competitiveness. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) was investigating Nvidia, without identifying the focus. Reuters reported on Friday, citing two people briefed on the matter, that SEC enforcement staff were examining potential accounting issues. Reuters said it could not determine when the SEC opened its inquiry or exactly what accounting issues it was examining. It noted that "investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing" and that many close without enforcement action. If confirmed, the probe would mark an expansion of regulatory scrutiny from export controls and national security concerns to Nvidia's financial reporting, potentially unsettling investor confidence in its financial transparency and earnings quality, according to market analysis. Nvidia shares closed down 14.01 percent at $125.53 on Friday, their steepest one-day fall since January 2025, capping their worst week since the 2008 financial crisis and a seventh straight weekly decline. The sell-off has wiped about $2.7 trillion off Nvidia's market value since its October peak, pushing the former world's most valuable company to fourth place behind Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet. The rout came despite record quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103 percent year-on-year, and a forecast of roughly $130 billion for the current quarter, underscoring concerns over the sustainability of Nvidia's growth amid mounting uncertainty. The accounting investigation would add to Nvidia's regulatory burden, although any finding of wrongdoing must await formal investigation and legal proceedings, He Weiwen, a senior fellow at the Center for China and Globalization, told the Global Times on Saturday. "Such investigations could take considerable time, leaving the company exposed to investor anxiety, selling pressure and further volatility," He said. "Even if no major wrongdoing is established, prolonged uncertainty could undermine confidence and disrupt business operations." The probe could also complicate Nvidia's leadership transition and raise corporate governance concerns, given that interim CEO Colette Kress previously oversaw the company's finances as chief financial officer, analysts said. The accounting inquiry adds to a widening web of investigations and regulatory scrutiny following the controversy involving former CEO Jensen Huang earlier this month, when he admitted having an affair. US authorities are investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed International over suspected violations of chip export controls, while Nvidia has established a board-level committee to oversee national security and export compliance. Washington has also extended its chip restrictions to Chinese companies' remote access to advanced US semiconductors, prompting a sharp response from China. The Chinese Foreign Ministry condemned the move as "typical economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction" and said China would take necessary measures to safeguard its legitimate rights and interests. Nvidia, meanwhile, said its limited H200 shipments to China were "legal and authorized" by US regulators after a licensing process lasting more than six months, with approvals subject to strict conditions and volume limits, according to the Associated Press. He Weiwen said Nvidia's troubles highlight the growing tension between Washington's national security priorities and US tech firms' commercial interests. “As technology competition with China becomes increasingly politicized, business decisions risk being driven by political considerations, potentially leaving companies to bear costs that could be difficult to reverse.” Huang's departure could further weaken Nvidia's ability to navigate these competing pressures, given his pivotal role in the company's rise as an AI powerhouse, extensive global business ties and longstanding advocacy for maintaining access to China's market, the expert added. President Donald Trump on Friday again backed Huang's potential return to Nvidia, calling him "one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world," although Nvidia's board has indicated it does not intend to reinstate him. On US chip export policy, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on the same day that H200 chips remained the "threshold level" permitted for sale to China and that he "wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy." He Weiwen said that while Washington has left the door open to limited chip exports to China, broader restrictions could still deprive US chipmakers of access to one of the world's fastest-growing AI markets, cutting into sales and revenue while accelerating China's development of domestic alternatives. Over time, this could reduce China's reliance on US technology and erode American chipmakers' global competitiveness, he warned. China continues to make gains in semiconductor manufacturing and advanced computing. Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (SMIC), China's largest contract chipmaker, reported a 123.4 percent year-on-year surge in third-quarter net profit attributable to shareholders, with revenue reaching a record $3.19 billion. In supercomputing, China's LineShine retained the top spot in the latest TOP500 ranking released on November 16. Despite fierce competition in advanced chips, China and the US still have room to cooperate. He Weiwen said "both sides should explore opportunities in semiconductors, AI governance, technical standards and research, echoing broader calls for international cooperation to drive innovation and ensure the stable growth of the global AI industry.

item.title: Anthropic rings the bell: Why were there no Chinese faces?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 00:07:00
File photo VCG On November 19, leading US AI company Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut in what was described as the largest IPO in history, with its market capitalization briefly climbing to nearly $2 trillion. However, among the seven founders who rang the opening bell at the ceremony, not a single Chinese face was present. Many netizens pointed out that while Chinese engineers had made indispensable contributions to Anthropic's growth, gaining access to its board and core decision-making circles remained extremely difficult. This has prompted questions about whether Chinese professionals being shut out of top decision-making positions is an unspoken "rule" in Silicon Valley. Chinese engineers are highly capable technically, but as a whole, they remain concentrated in frontline research and engineering roles, with limited opportunities to advance into the highest levels of corporate decision-making. This is a common problem among US technology companies. Data from US think tanks such as MacroPolo show that, at one point, Chinese researchers (based on undergraduate degrees) accounted for around 38 percent of top-tier AI researchers in the US. In some years, researchers from China even outnumbered those from the US among top-tier AI researchers worldwide. Chinese researchers and engineers are also well represented on the initial team at Meta's Superintelligence Labs and among key research contributors at OpenAI and Anthropic. The technological foundations of these companies rely heavily on Chinese engineers and researchers, while decision-making power remains largely in the hands of founding teams and established networks. There is even a specific term for this phenomenon: the "bamboo ceiling." The stark contrast between Silicon Valley's heavy reliance on Chinese technical talent and the limited representation of Chinese professionals in its top decision-making circles also undermines the Silicon Valley myth that technical excellence alone guarantees equal rewards. Leading technology companies and elite circles have long prided themselves on being "diverse and inclusive." Yet this inclusiveness is, to a considerable extent, reserved for the privileged. From the early days of the semiconductor industry to today's cutting-edge fields of large AI models, computing power and algorithms, numerous Chinese researchers have contributed their expertise. Yet they are often confined to the role of "technical contributors", rarely taking center stage at milestone moments such as IPO bell-ringing events or strategic decision-making forums - platforms that symbolize recognition and a voice in decision-making. This points to a long-standing structural barrier. In recent years, the environment for Chinese technology professionals in Western countries has deteriorated markedly. Prejudice once concealed beneath the rhetoric of "free movement of talent" has increasingly surfaced under the guise of "national security." This policy-level distrust, compounded by heightened scrutiny based on identity amid geopolitical tensions, has further narrowed opportunities for Chinese professionals to advance. In the wake of the controversy surrounding Jensen Huang, some Western media outlets have openly spread the false claim that "all Chinese are spies," fueling anti-China and anti-Chinese rhetoric. In such an atmosphere, Chinese professionals may still be automatically branded as "untrustworthy," no matter how impressive their professional achievements are. At the core of competition for talent is respect for and fair treatment of innovators. An advantage built on suspicion, barriers and exclusionary networks cannot last. Recently, news that Liu Jun, a member of the US National Academy of Sciences, had returned to China to take up a teaching position caused a stir in US public opinion. There is little reason to be surprised. Talent naturally gravitates toward places where the environment is more open, policies are more stable and support systems are more comprehensive. That is simply how the world works.

item.title: 'Thank You, China' from world leaders is more than just a courtesy: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 00:00:00
This photo taken on November 16, 2026 shows a view of Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province with APEC elements. China will hold the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen from November 18 to 19. Photo: VCG Behind the widely shared expressions of "Thank you, China" lies not only an expectation of further cooperation, but also a vote of confidence in China as a reliable partner. As the host, China patiently built bridges of communication, responding to major economies' concerns over industrial chain stability and technological innovation while listening to the pressing needs of developing members for infrastructure, capacity building and green transition. The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting has successfully concluded. Before heading home, leaders from various economies expressed their sincere gratitude to Chinese President Xi Jinping, China, the host of this meeting, and the city of Shenzhen. Russian President Vladimir Putin said he "congratulates" Chinese friends' hosting of a "very successful APEC summit." US President Donald Trump said that if the highest possible score were 10, he would give his visit to China "a 12." Leaders from Vietnam, South Korea, Malaysia, Thailand and Canada, as well as representatives of international organizations and other participants, also spoke highly of the achievements of China's APEC Year and expressed their appreciation for the excellent work of the Chinese side. It is hard to say goodbye after a visit to Shenzhen. The Shenzhen APEC meeting has left a distinctive mark on the history of APEC and a lasting impression on the hearts and minds of participating economies across the Asia-Pacific. During the Shenzhen meeting, leaders of various economies created many heartwarming moments as they stepped out of conference venues and into the city's streets. Beyond the meeting rooms, the streets of Shenzhen became places for unexpected encounters. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, whose ancestral roots trace back to Guangdong Province, showed off his Cantonese skills on several occasions. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese sampled beef at a supermarket, while Mexico's Secretary of Health David Kershenobich Stalnikowitz visited Huaqiangbei, a bustling commercial district popular with international visitors. These heartwarming moments not only became trending topics on Chinese social media, but also left fond memories for guests from various sides who had traveled from afar. Behind the widely shared expressions of "Thank you, China" lies not only an expectation of further cooperation, but also a vote of confidence in China as a reliable partner. At a time when protectionism is on the rise and global economic growth is under pressure, bringing 21 APEC member economies together around the same table is no easy task. This is all the more challenging given the vast differences in their economic size, stages of development and diverse interests. An equal platform for dialogue and in-depth discussion is therefore all the more necessary. As the host, China patiently built bridges of communication, responding to major economies' concerns over industrial chain stability and technological innovation while listening to the pressing needs of developing members in infrastructure, capacity building and green transition. Leaders from various economies consistently praised China's thoughtful and efficient organization, as well as the candid and pragmatic atmosphere for communication. The meeting also forged tangible consensus. From the Suzhou Statement at the APEC Ministers Responsible for Trade Meeting to the Chengdu Statement at the APEC Digital and AI Ministerial Meeting, from the Nanjing Statement at the APEC Human Resources Development Ministerial Meeting to 2026 APEC Leaders' Shenzhen Outlook at the Economic Leaders' Meeting, China placed economic and trade cooperation, innovation and people's livelihoods at the heart of its year-long APEC agenda. A total of 321 meetings and events and 75 major deliverables have provided more concrete avenues for Asia-Pacific cooperation, injecting fresh vitality and strong momentum into regional development. Some foreign media outlets have noted that, against a backdrop of mounting global geopolitical tensions, the Shenzhen meeting was one of the "few forums" capable of bringing "together" economies of different sizes. These achievements reflect the host's year-long commitment and demonstrate that, by identifying common interests, economies can continue to unleash the vitality and potential of the Asia-Pacific economy and advance the building of an Asia-Pacific community. Many leaders and foreign media outlets have praised Shenzhen, remarking that every time they come, it looks different. Shenzhen itself also offers the world a glimpse of how China is advancing high-standard opening-up. Having grown amid China's reform and opening-up, Shenzhen has now become a key node in global industrial chains and innovation networks. By hosting the APEC meeting in Shenzhen and announcing new funding for APEC practical cooperation to launch new cooperation institutions covering digital technology, cross-border data flow, clean energy, and the development of SMEs, China shows its sincerity in committing resources and sharing development opportunities. Asia-Pacific economies vary widely in their stages of development. Some prioritize market access, while others are in urgent need of infrastructure and talent. China brings these diverse needs into a single cooperation agenda, enabling all parties to find pathways for participation. This vision carries substantial practical weight. The trust that Asia-Pacific partners place in China also stems from China's strategic resolve to take root in the Asia-Pacific, contribute to its development and deliver benefits to the region. China outlined the way forward in Shenzhen, facilitated agreement among all parties on concrete actions, and readied resources and platforms to implement those actions. These efforts have shown all parties that China is willing to listen to the concerns of different economies, has the ability to coordinate their respective interests, and demonstrates a sense of responsibility in advancing shared goals. Against narratives that frame economic ties as burdens and interdependence as risks, China continues to expand openness for the long-term interests of the entire Asia-Pacific. The dynamism of the Asia-Pacific economy stems from decades of close exchanges between people and enterprises. To preserve these connections is to safeguard shared opportunities for growth. Further recognition of the Shenzhen APEC meeting will translate into easier trade, smoother exchanges and broader access to innovative opportunities ahead. The gratitude expressed to China by participants in Shenzhen grows out of trust built through cooperation. China's actions over the year demonstrate that the more complex the international landscape becomes, the more the Asia-Pacific can find a sincere, reliable and capable leader on the path of open cooperation.

item.title: Chinese boys, aged 14 and 3, set BMX and cartwheel records for Guinness World Records Day
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-20 17:28:00
Liu Haoran November 19 marked the 22nd annual Guinness World Records Day. Challengers from around the world pushed the limits of human capability once again on the same day. Among them, two challengers from China attracted considerable attention: a 14-year-old who performed 10 consecutive flips in the air while riding a BMX bike, and a 3-year-old who performed 55 cartwheels in one minute on the ground. In China, 14-year-old BMX freestyle rider Liu Haoran set two records during this year's Guinness World Records Day challenge: "Most consecutive BMX side somersaults" (10 consecutive flips) and "Highest BMX backflip" (3.13 meters). Liu also improved on his own previous world record. A BMX backflip is a freestyle trick in which the rider and bike rotate 360 degrees backward mid-air off a ramp or jump before landing on the wheels. The flair is a highly difficult maneuver in BMX freestyle. Riders must launch themselves into the air on a ramp, simultaneously flipping themselves and their bikes sideways before landing precisely back down the ramp. Peng Yizhou The other challenger from China, Peng Yizhou, 3, a martial arts school student, completed 55 sidecar flips in one minute during this year's challenge, setting a Guinness World Record for the most cartwheels in one minute in the under 16 category. Peng was born in Tangyin County, Anyang City, Central China's Henan Province. His parents are both martial arts instructors. From the age of 7 months, Peng lived with his parents at a martial arts school, watching the older students practice martial arts. At the age of 2, he began to imitate cartwheels on his own and gradually learned to perform the movement independently under his father's guidance. In addition to cartwheels, he also enjoys swimming, playing with toys, and participating in activities with the older students at the martial arts school. For Peng, the cartwheel wasn't initially a competitive skill he needed to master; rather, it stemmed from curiosity and imitation of his surroundings. His parents recalled that when Peng first completed a cartwheel independently, he tried repeatedly, falling several times, until finally landing steadily and excitedly turning to his father, shouting, "Dad, I stood up!" item.title: Time for Takaichi to retract her erroneous 'survival-threatening situation' remarks
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-20 12:35:00
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi speaks to reporters ahead of her departure for a tour of Europe at the Prime Minister's Official Residence in Tokyo on June 13, 2026. Photo: VCG On November 19, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi held a press conference after attending the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, reiterating that Japan's basic position on the Taiwan question remains consistent with the 1972 Sino-Japanese Joint Statement and emphasizing that "there has been absolutely no change to this position." She also said that "China is an important neighboring country," that the status of the four political documents as the "basic documents on Japan-China relations" remains unchanged, and that Japan is willing to comprehensively advance a strategic relationship of mutual benefit through dialogue and build "constructive and stable" China-Japan relations. However, when asked about with her erroneous remarks a year earlier that the Chinese mainland's "use of force on Taiwan" could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, Takaichi continued to evade the question, saying that "she could not comment on hypothetical scenarios." The core principles of the Sino-Japanese Joint Statement are clearly set out in black and white: The Government of Japan recognizes that the Government of the People's Republic of China as the sole legal Government of China. The Government of the People's Republic of China reiterates that Taiwan is an inalienable part of the territory of the People's Republic of China. The Government of Japan fully understands and respects this stand of the Government of the People's Republic of China, and it firmly maintains its stand under Article 8 of the Postdam Proclamation. This statement, together with the other four political documents, including the Treaty of Peace and Friendship between China and Japan, forms the political foundation for the normalization of diplomatic relations between the two countries. These are commitments that both countries must uphold in their bilateral relations and an important part of the postwar international order. Linking a "contingency in Taiwan" to a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan and implying that Japan might exercise its right to collective self-defense directly undermines the framework established by the 1972 Sino-Japanese Joint Statement and seriously deviates from the postwar international order that Japan, as a defeated nation in World War II, is obliged to observe. If Japan's position on the Taiwan question is truly consistent with the Sino-Japan Joint Statement, it should acknowledge its mistake and publicly retract the provocative claim that "a Taiwan contingency is a Japan contingency." On the same day, the leaders of China, Russia and the US held a historic trilateral meeting in Shenzhen and issued the China-Russia-US Heads of State Declaration toward Peace. All three leaders recalled the history of their countries fighting side by side during World War II, sending an important signal of their shared commitment to safeguarding the postwar international order - a message that Tokyo should take note of. The core documents underpinning the postwar international order include the Cairo Declaration and the Potsdam Proclamation, which made clear that Japan must return the Chinese territories it had seized, including Taiwan. Japan accepted the Potsdam Proclamation and surrendered unconditionally, and subsequently reaffirmed its commitment to adhering to Article 8 of the proclamation in the Sino-Japan Joint Statement. Any remarks that directly link the Taiwan question to Japan's security, or even imply possible military intervention, constitute an open challenge to the outcomes of the victory in World War II and the postwar international order. China-Japan relations remain strained over remarks concerning Taiwan, with tensions already affecting economic and trade ties, people-to-people exchanges and other areas. Takaichi has emphasized dialogue and a strategic relationship of mutual benefit, but her words must be matched by actions. If she sincerely wishes to improve China-Japan relations, retracting her erroneous remarks should be the first step. Otherwise, merely repeating that Japan's "position remains unchanged" without making substantive corrections will do little to inspire confidence or benefit Japan itself, or contribute to lasting peace and stability in the region.
